introduction: Tasks currently disappear with the process. A database moves state outside that process, but introduces a new boundary: connectivity, schema, transactions and recovery can now fail independently.

This week runs a real PostgreSQL database, applies explicit migrations and proves that task data survives an app restart. The integration tests use a separate disposable database. A mock cannot establish the SQL behavior being taught.
prerequisites: Week 5's Docker client/server and Compose v2 work.
Use ~/dev-opps-lab/app/taskboard with its activated Python venv and the supplied Compose file.
Stop the week-5 container so port 8000 is available. Use only synthetic local data.

concepts.title: A table is a contract for stored state
paragraphs: The tasks table stores a UUID primary key, owner, title, completion flag and timestamps. A primary key prevents duplicate identity. NOT NULL rejects missing required values. CHECK constraints reject states that should never exist, such as a completed task without a completion time.

Application validation provides useful client errors, but database constraints protect the stored invariant even if another writer bypasses that validation. A migration is a versioned change to this schema. Editing an already-applied migration can make history disagree with reality; add a new migration instead.
concepts.example: The completion_consistent constraint requires completed_at to be null before completion and at least created_at after completion.
concepts.judgment: Keep the business invariant explicit at both boundaries where it matters. Do not assume Python tests prove database enforcement.

concepts.title: Transactions make related changes succeed or fail together
paragraphs: A transaction groups database operations. Commit makes the successful changes durable under the database's configured guarantees; rollback discards an uncommitted attempt. The reference uses context-managed transactions so exceptions do not leave half-applied work.

Concurrency adds another question: two requests can read and update at almost the same time. The completion operation must preserve its first timestamp under concurrent completion, not just when called twice in a single-threaded test.
concepts.example: A failed migration must not record its version while leaving only half its statements applied.
concepts.judgment: Test the failure path against actual PostgreSQL. Replacing the database with a fake removes the boundary you need evidence about.

concepts.title: Started, ready and persistent are separate properties
paragraphs: A running database container may still be initializing. The Compose database healthcheck waits for PostgreSQL to accept connections. The migrate service then applies schema changes before app startup. A successful dependency startup check does not guarantee the dependency will stay available.

The named development volume outlives app replacement and ordinary container recreation. A volume is not a backup: deletion, bad writes or corruption can affect it. The test database uses a different name and disposable storage so test cleanup cannot silently target development data.
concepts.example: /livez can remain 200 while /readyz and task operations report 503 after a database outage.
concepts.judgment: Use liveness to avoid unnecessary restart loops and readiness to control whether a dependency-dependent service can accept useful traffic.

steps.title: Prepare private credentials and select the database stage
steps.purpose: The initializer creates .env once without printing its random values. Existing .env is retained; do not paste it into evidence.

commands.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab/app/taskboard
source .venv/bin/activate
if test ! -f .env; then python tools/init_lab.py || exit 1; fi
python - <<'PY' || exit 1
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('.env')
text = p.read_text()
assert 'TASKBOARD_STAGE=07' in text or 'TASKBOARD_STAGE=06' in text
p.write_text(text.replace('TASKBOARD_STAGE=07', 'TASKBOARD_STAGE=06'))
PY
git check-ignore .env
explain: cd and source select the project/interpreter. init_lab.py creates random credentials with exclusive creation and Linux mode 0600; if it says the file exists, retain it and continue.
The short Python edit reads only this local file and changes the non-secret stage selector from 07 to 06. It does not print the file.
git check-ignore confirms .env is excluded; if it is not, fix the ignore rule before committing anything.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
commands.expected: Stage 06 is selected and git check-ignore prints .env.
commands.troubleshoot: An existing-file message from the initializer is protective, not a request to delete credentials. Check the stage line with grep '^TASKBOARD_STAGE=' .env, never cat the whole file.

steps.checkpoint: Explain which account owns tasks in stage 6: local-student, before the two-user stage.

steps.title: Read the schema and start dependencies in order
steps.purpose: Compose supplies the complete database, migration and app configuration locally. It publishes only the app's loopback port.

commands.code:
cat migrations/001_tasks.sql
cat migrations/002_owner_order.sql
docker compose up --build -d app
docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail 30 migrate
curl --fail --show-error --retry 10 --retry-connrefused --retry-delay 1 --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:8000/readyz || exit 1
explain: cat displays the CREATE TABLE constraints and the compatible index migration.
up --build -d app builds the runtime and starts required services in dependency order. -d leaves them running in the background.
ps shows their state; logs inspects the explicit migration. curl verifies application readiness, not just container startup.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
Retry applies only to this bounded, read-only readiness/liveness request so asynchronous startup is not confused with a service failure; it does not retry task creation.
commands.expected: Database healthy, migrate exits successfully, app becomes ready. The schema contains constraints and an owner/order index.
commands.troubleshoot: If migration fails, inspect its sanitized error before starting the app manually. A listening database with the wrong schema is not ready for this app.

steps.checkpoint: Explain the primary key, owner filter, title constraint and completion consistency rule in your own words.

steps.title: Prove persistence across app replacement
steps.purpose: Save a response as evidence, restart only the application, and compare the same actual task ID.

commands.code:
mkdir -p reports
curl --fail --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Persist through app restart"}' http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks > reports/week06-created.json || exit 1
docker compose restart app
curl --fail --show-error --retry 10 --retry-connrefused --retry-delay 1 --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:8000/readyz
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks > reports/week06-after.json
python - <<'PY' || exit 1
import json
from pathlib import Path
before = json.loads(Path('reports/week06-created.json').read_text())
after = json.loads(Path('reports/week06-after.json').read_text())
assert before in after['items']
print('Original task, including timestamps, survived the app restart.')
PY
explain: mkdir prepares a report directory; the POST writes its JSON response to a file without echoing private configuration.
restart app replaces the running process without deleting the database volume. The bounded readiness read waits for useful service.
The list response is captured separately. Python loads both JSON documents and asserts the full original task is present; a missing or changed task fails the assertion.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
Retry applies only to this bounded, read-only readiness/liveness request so asynchronous startup is not confused with a service failure; it does not retry task creation.
commands.expected: The assertion passes for the same task ID, title and timestamps.
commands.troubleshoot: If the POST failed, do not treat an empty saved file as evidence. Inspect the HTTP error first.

steps.checkpoint: State exactly which failure this proves survival of, and why it does not yet prove backup recovery.

steps.title: Exercise the real SQL boundary
steps.purpose: Read the test before running it. The fixture permits only the dedicated test database and creates a uniquely named schema per case.

commands.code:
sed -n '1,220p' tests/integration/conftest.py
docker compose --profile test run --build --rm integration
explain: sed prints a bounded portion of the integration fixture so you can inspect its target guards and cleanup.
--profile test enables test services. run --build --rm builds and executes the integration test container, returns its test exit status and removes that one-off container.
commands.expected: Tests connect to taskboard_test and exercise real SQL constraints, transaction rollback, concurrent completion and migration behavior.
commands.troubleshoot: If tests skip or cannot connect, that is missing database evidence. Inspect test-db health and the fixture's rejection message; never redirect it to taskboard to get it running.

steps.checkpoint: Pick one SQL constraint test and explain why a memory mock could not establish the same behavior.

failure.title: The app points to a nonexistent database host
failure.boundary: This overrides only the app's database URL in this Compose project. It leaves the development volume and database process intact.

inject.code:
cat > compose.week06-fault.yaml <<'YAML'
services:
  app:
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://taskboard:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@wrong-db:5432/taskboard
YAML
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.week06-fault.yaml up -d --no-deps --force-recreate app
explain: The quoted here-document writes a literal Compose override; Compose later substitutes the password locally without printing it.
-f selects the base and override. --no-deps affects only app; --force-recreate applies its changed environment.
inject.expected: The app process starts but cannot resolve wrong-db for database operations.
inject.troubleshoot: Do not run docker compose config into shared evidence: expanded configuration can contain credentials.

investigate.code:
curl --include --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:8000/livez
curl --include --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:8000/readyz
curl --include --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks
docker compose ps db
explain: Compare process-only liveness with database-dependent readiness and task behavior.
ps db checks whether the actual database remains healthy.
investigate.expected: Liveness 200; readiness/task operations bounded 503; the real db remains healthy.
investigate.troubleshoot: If liveness also fails, inspect app startup before attributing the symptom to dependency connectivity.

hints: Compare the service name db with the override's hostname.
Healthy database state does not prove the app is configured to reach it.

explanation: The database is present, but the app targets a different name. Repair the app configuration and recreate it. No database deletion or schema reset is needed.

explain: With no fault -f file, Compose uses the original configuration and recreates only the app.
recover.expected: The app returns to the intended db hostname.
recover.troubleshoot: Check that COMPOSE_FILE is not overriding the file selection in your shell if behavior differs.

explain: Verify readiness and retained tasks using the repaired app.
Retry applies only to this bounded, read-only readiness/liveness request so asynchronous startup is not confused with a service failure; it does not retry task creation.
verification.expected: Ready response and the original task data.
verification.troubleshoot: If tasks are missing, inspect stage and database identity; do not assume connectivity recovery proves data correctness.

questions.prompt: Why should a migration run separately from every app startup?
questions.answer: Schema changes need controlled ordering, identity and failure handling. Running them in every process creates contention and hides deployment decisions. The explicit migration job records a distinct result before the app depends on that schema.

questions.prompt: Why is a named volume not a backup?
questions.hint: What happens after a bad write?
questions.answer: It preserves current data across container replacement, including mistakes. Recovery needs a separate usable copy and a tested restore procedure, which the capstone will establish.

questions.prompt: Why reject a test URL pointing at taskboard?
questions.hint: What does the fixture do during cleanup?
questions.answer: Tests deliberately create and destroy data/schema. A dedicated database-name guard prevents configuration mistakes from turning test cleanup into development or production data loss. Isolation is part of test correctness.

exercise.brief: Add one real-database test for a stored invariant, and prove it catches an intentional defect in an isolated test schema.
constraints: Use the guarded test database only.
Do not edit applied development migrations or weaken constraints globally.
deliverables: Test code, a failing result and repaired passing result, plus a transaction explanation.
acceptance: The test sends real SQL through the reference store/connection.
It fails for the intended invariant and cleans only its own schema.
hints: A completed task without completed_at violates the supplied table check.
solution: In the isolated fixture transaction, attempt the invalid row and assert PostgreSQL rejects it.
Rollback the failed transaction before further queries; verify no invalid row was committed.
Run the complete integration suite after restoring the intended implementation.

explain: Stop only this course Compose project's services while preserving its development volume and files. Do not add --volumes.
cleanup.expected: Containers stop; data remains for week 7.
cleanup.troubleshoot: Use docker compose ps -a to inspect stopped containers if needed.

references.title: Compose startup ordering
references.usedFor: Health-dependent startup and explicit migration ordering.
